steps.say: A niche by the hearth: the Lar of the family, dancing with his drinking horn; the Penates who keep the store cupboard; the snake of the house's Genius painted below.

steps.rite: Every morning, before anything else, the small rite.
order: Wash your hands
Lay a garland on the shrine
Drop salted meal into the lamp's flame
Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.restart: You stop, and begin again. Postumia is watching from the loom, and says the words with you.
steps.done: The flame takes the meal with a small crackle. The house is kept.

steps.end: It is small and it is daily, and it ties this house to every Roman house since the kings.

steps.say: Every house in Rome prayed harder after Cannae. Sulpicia lost two brothers there. She stands behind you and makes sure you do it exactly.

order: Wash your hands
Lay a garland on the shrine
Drop salted meal into the lamp's flame
Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.restart: You begin again. It must be right.
steps.done: The Lar dances in the lamplight. The house is kept.

steps.end: Duty to the gods, to the family, to Rome: it is one duty, begun here, at the hearth.

steps.say: The shrine is painted now, like everything Valeria paid for. She doesn't come to it. The boy's nurse does, for luck.

order: Wash your hands

Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.slack: You slip, and go on anyway. Who's to know?
steps.done: The flame takes the meal. From Valeria's room, laughter.

steps.end: Valeria's Egyptian has his own gods. She keeps them in her bedroom.

steps.say: Beside the Lares Flavia has put a silver bust of the Emperor. Everyone has one. It seems wise.

order: Wash your hands
Lay a garland on the shrine
Drop salted meal into the lamp's flame
Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.done: The flame takes the meal. The Emperor's bust looks on.

steps.end: Flavia has not come to the household gods in years. The slaves do, for luck, when she isn't looking.

steps.say: The Emperor's laws are against sacrifice. They don't yet name the little household gods; in a few years they will, down to a pinch of incense in a shrine.
Rufina is a Christian, and pays the bishop. She has seen your shrine.

steps.ask: She says nothing. She looks at the Lar, and at you.

options.text: Keep it, and do the rite
Put it away in the chest
options.say: You wrap the Lar in a cloth and put him away. The niche is empty.

order: Wash your hands

Drop salted meal into the lamp's flame
Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.done: The flame takes the meal. Rufina has shut her door.

gain.ledger: Kept the household gods when your wife turned away.

steps.end: Everything is changing in Rome. Some things you choose to keep.

steps.say: The Lar is behind a curtain. The Vandals didn't want him: bronze too little to bother with.

steps.rite: The morning rite, behind the curtain.
order: Wash your hands
Lay a garland on the shrine
Drop salted meal into the lamp's flame
Pour a drop of wine
Say: be kind to this house
wrong: Turn your back on the shrine
steps.slack: You slip, and go on. There's no one left to be exact for.

steps.end: The house is half empty. Nobody has come to mend the door. Nobody will.

steps.say: The niche is empty. Galla sold him with the candlesticks.

steps.end: You leave a pinch of meal in the empty niche anyway.

lararium_fall.title: The household gods
lararium_fall.where: What is left of your house, AD 552

steps.say: The roof fell in the second siege. The niche is still there, and the painted snake, and the Lar in his cloth at the bottom of the chest.

steps.hold: Set him in the niche and pour the last of the water for him.
steps.done: He dances, as he always did, in the rubble.

gain.ledger: Kept the household gods in the ruined city.

steps.end: A thousand years of mornings, and this one.

steps.say: The niche is there, and the painted snake. The Lar is not: your wife sold him a hundred years ago, in another life.

steps.end: A thousand years of mornings, and none left.

steps.say: You sleep on a straw mattress. At first light the cocks crow all over the seven hills.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep. At first light the carts are already on the Sacred Way.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep, as much as anyone sleeps in the Subura: the drunks, the dogs, a fight on the stairs.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep, badly. Carts are only allowed in the city at night, and they are all under your window.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep. Before dawn you hear the psalms from the church at the end of the street.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep with a knife under the mattress, like everyone.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: You sleep in the corner where the roof still holds. Owls in the Forum.

steps.end: Morning.

steps.say: Nothing public is done in Rome without the auspices: no vote, no battle, no law. The augur marks out a square of sky with his curved staff.

steps.pick: You stand in the augurs' place on the Arx, facing south. An eagle crosses from your left, from the east. For a Roman augur, is that a good sign?
options: Yes: for Romans the left is the lucky side
No: the left is always unlucky
steps.yes: Yes. The Greeks face north and call the right lucky; the Romans face south, and it's the left.
steps.no: A Roman augur faces south, and the left, the east, is the lucky side.

steps.pick: A raven calls on your right, and a crow on your left. What is that?
steps.yes: Favourable. The augurs' books say so.
steps.no: The books say: a raven on the right and a crow on the left is favourable.

steps.end: The augur tells the consul the gods allow it. He was watching you. You'll learn.
The augur nods at you. The consul may go ahead. The gods and Rome agree.

steps.say: The consul waits for the sign before he marches for Macedonia. In this war the gods are listened to.

steps.say: A consul who wants to stop an assembly announces he is watching the sky for signs. Then no vote may be held. Bibulus stopped Caesar that way for a year, sitting at home.

steps.ask: A tribune's man asks you to report thunder on the left: it will stop tomorrow's vote.

options.say: You report thunder. There was none. The vote is stopped.
options.ledger: Reported a false omen to stop a vote.

steps.end: The auspices still decide everything. That's why everyone lies about them.

steps.say: The augurs are still appointed: noble young men, and the Emperor is one. It's an honour, like a seat at the games.

steps.end: The augur has a dinner to go to. He thanks you for your company.

steps.say: The haruspex is an Etruscan, as they always are. The Senate sends for his order when there are prodigies: a calf with two heads, a statue sweating blood.

steps.pick: The haruspex holds up a sheep's liver. The bronze liver of Piacenza shows its regions, each a god's. The lobe called the head is missing. What does that mean?
options: Disaster: a liver without its head
steps.yes: Disaster. Before Marcellus died in ambush, his victim's liver had no head.
steps.no: A liver without its head means disaster: Marcellus's had none the day before he died.

steps.pick: The gall bladder is swollen on the enemy's side. What does he tell the general?
steps.yes: Harm on the enemy's side is harm to the enemy.
steps.no: The enemy's side: harm to the enemy. Good.

steps.end: "Stick to your trade," the haruspex says. "Leave the gods' livers to us."
The haruspex looks at you with more respect. "Your grandmother was from Tarquinii?" he asks.

steps.say: The haruspex is not allowed into private houses: Constantine's law. He may read livers only in public, at the temples, for the state. Few ask him now.

steps.end: He wraps the liver in a cloth. "My father had the Senate's ear," he says. "I have this."

steps.say: A woman stops you. A man cheated her of her savings and she can't write. She has a sheet of lead and a nail.

steps.ask: "Write it for me," she says. "Name him to the gods below. Then we fold it and nail it, and drop it in the water."

options.say: "Then I'll find someone who can," she says.

steps.type: I bind Gaius Vettius, his hands, his tongue, his sleep, to the gods below.
steps.good: The letters are clear. The gods will read them.
steps.bad: Scratchy. She says the gods can read a scratch, if it's meant.

steps.hold: Fold the lead, and drive the nail through it.
steps.done: She drops it into the fountain. It sinks at once.

gain.ledger: Wrote a curse tablet and dropped it in a fountain.

steps.end: There are thousands of them in the wells and fountains of Rome. The gods below must be very busy.

steps.say: The keeper of {temple} sells small offerings at the steps: incense, a cake, a clay figure of a body part to be healed.

options.say: The smoke goes up past the columns.
You lay it on the altar. A priest will eat it later.

options.text: A vow: something if your wish is granted
options.say: You say it quietly. The keeper nods: a vow is a contract.
options.ledger: Made a vow at a temple.

steps.end: {god} has been here longer than anyone's grandfather's grandfather. The steps are worn by knees.
